title: Puranas and the Bhakti Poets
bigQuestion: How did the Puranas and the bhakti poets bring Hindu devotion into everyday languages and lives?

story.title: The Queen Who Sang
story.kicker: A royal woman leaves the palace singing, and people across India sing her songs back.
paragraphs: Rajasthan, in the early 1500s. Stories say a young woman named Mira was married into a royal family. Since childhood she had loved Krishna. She called him her true husband and sang to him day and night.

Her in-laws were not pleased. A royal wife was supposed to stay behind palace walls. Mira danced in temples with wandering holy people. She sang in the everyday language of the people, not in Sanskrit. Stories say her family tried to stop her, even to harm her, but she was protected.

At last, the stories say, Mira left the palace. She traveled to Vrindavan, the land of Krishna's childhood, and later to Dwarka on the western coast. Wherever she went, she sang, and crowds gathered to listen and sing with her.

Historians can confirm only some details of Mira's life. The songs, though, are real and alive. Hundreds of songs carry her name. People across North India sing them at home, at temples and in concerts today. They call her Mirabai.

Mirabai was one of many poet-saints of bhakti, loving devotion. Some were kings and queens. Others were weavers, tailors, farmers or cobblers. They sang in their own languages, and their songs traveled farther than any palace order.
story.think: Why do you think Mirabai's songs spread so widely, even though she left the palace behind?

lessons.title: Old Stories, Big Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Puranas are large collections of stories, cosmology and worship, composed over many centuries.
reading: Where does the story of Prahlad come from? Or Krishna lifting a mountain? Or Durga defeating a buffalo demon? Many come from the *Puranas*. Purana means old, and these texts tell ancient tales.

Tradition counts eighteen major Puranas, the Mahapuranas, and many minor ones. They include creation stories, family lines of gods and kings, descriptions of the universe, and rules for worship and pilgrimage. Tradition often names Vyasa as their arranger.

Scholars date most of the Puranas to about 300–1500 CE, with much growth during and after the Gupta period. Each one often favors one deity. Some center on Vishnu, some on Shiva, some on the Goddess. They are part of smriti.

one of the eighteen major Puranas
ideas about how the universe is made and ordered

lessons.title: The Bhagavata and the Devi Mahatmya
lessons.mainIdea: The Bhagavata Purana tells Krishna's life, and the Devi Mahatmya praises the Goddess.
reading: The *Bhagavata Purana* is among the most loved Puranas. Its tenth book tells of Krishna's childhood in Vraja: stealing butter, lifting Govardhana hill to shelter the villagers, and dancing with the gopis, the cowherd women.
For many Vaishnavas, the Bhagavata is a central scripture. It teaches bhakti through stories. Scholars often date it to about the 9th–10th century CE, and many link it to South Indian devotion.

The *Devi Mahatmya*, part of the Markandeya Purana, praises the Goddess. It tells how Durga defeats Mahishasura and other demons. Shakta Hindus recite it, especially during Navaratri. It presents the Goddess as the supreme power of the universe.

words.d: a Purana devoted to Vishnu, especially Krishna's life
'Glory of the Goddess', a text praising Durga, part of the Markandeya Purana

lessons.title: The Ten Avatars of Vishnu
lessons.mainIdea: The Puranas describe Vishnu descending as avatars, and a common list names ten.
reading: The Gita says that whenever dharma declines, the Lord comes into the world to protect the good (Gita 4.7–8). The Puranas tell how Vishnu does this as an *avatar*, meaning one who descends.

A common list names ten avatars: Matsya the fish, Kurma the tortoise, Varaha the boar, Narasimha the man-lion, Vamana the dwarf, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, the Buddha or Balarama, and Kalki, who is yet to come.

Lists differ. The Bhagavata names more than twenty. Some lists include the Buddha, others Balarama. Vaishnavas honor these avatars as Vishnu himself, and some see Krishna as the source of all avatars.

lessons.title: What Is Bhakti?
lessons.mainIdea: Bhakti is loving devotion to God, and it became a movement of poet-saints across India.
reading: The Gita already praises *bhakti*, loving devotion. From about the 6th century CE, it became a wave of song. Poet-saints sang to Shiva, Vishnu, Krishna, Rama and the Goddess, in their own languages rather than Sanskrit.

Bhakti poets often spoke to God like a friend, a parent, a child or a beloved. They taught that love matters more than ritual rules or high birth. Many came from groups that were barred from Vedic learning.

Bhakti began in the Tamil south and spread north over centuries. It shaped temple worship, festivals and home devotion. Much Hindu practice today, like singing bhajans or kirtan, grows from this movement.

words.d: loving devotion to God
a devotional poet honored as holy by followers
a devotional song, often sung together

lessons.title: The Alvars and Nayanars
lessons.mainIdea: In Tamil lands, the Alvars sang to Vishnu and the Nayanars sang to Shiva, c. 6th–9th centuries CE.
reading: Between about the 6th and 9th centuries CE, twelve *Alvars* sang to Vishnu in Tamil. Their songs were gathered into the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, the four thousand divine hymns. Sri Vaishnavas, followers of Ramanuja, honor it like a Tamil Veda.

At the same time, sixty-three *Nayanars* sang to Shiva. Their hymns form part of the Tirumurai, a sacred collection for Tamil Shaivas. Songs by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar are sung in Shiva temples today.

These poet-saints came from many backgrounds. Andal was a woman poet among the Alvars. Tiruppan Alvar came from a caste of singers who were kept out of temples. Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a woman among the Nayanars.

words.d: twelve Tamil poet-saints devoted to Vishnu

lessons.title: Across Caste Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Bhakti poets often challenged caste barriers, though caste did not disappear.
reading: Stories of the poet-saints often show devotion crossing caste lines. Tiruppan Alvar was not allowed into the temple at Srirangam. A story says a priest carried him in on his shoulders at the god's command.

In Maharashtra, the poet-saint Chokhamela was from a caste treated as untouchable. His songs ask why he must stand outside the temple. Ravidas, a leatherworker poet in North India, sang that God loves the humble. His songs are in the Sikh Guru Granth Sahib.
Historians note that bhakti did not end caste. Many temples still barred people for centuries. But the poet-saints gave voice to people often left out, and later reformers drew on their songs.

words.d: a 14th-century Marathi poet-saint from a caste treated as untouchable

lessons.title: Mirabai
lessons.mainIdea: Mirabai, a 16th-century Rajput woman devoted to Krishna, is one of the best-loved bhakti poets.
reading: *Mirabai* lived in Rajasthan in the 1500s. Tradition says she was married into a royal family but gave her heart to Krishna. She sang in a mix of Rajasthani and Braj, languages the people spoke.

Her songs speak to Krishna as her beloved. They show longing, joy and courage. Many describe her refusal to follow rules that kept her from worship. Scholars note that many songs under her name were added by later singers.

Mirabai became a symbol. Gandhi admired her courage. Women across India have seen her as a model of following one's calling. Her bhajans are sung today in homes, temples and concert halls, including in Illinois.

words.d: a 16th-century Rajput poet-saint devoted to Krishna

lessons.title: Kabir, Claimed by Many
lessons.mainIdea: Kabir, a 15th-century weaver poet of Varanasi, is claimed by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs.
reading: *Kabir* was a weaver in Varanasi in the 1400s. Tradition says he was raised in a Muslim family and learned from a Hindu teacher, Ramananda. He sang short, sharp verses called dohas.
Kabir mocked empty ritual in both Hindu and Muslim practice. He sang that God is found within, not in temple or mosque. He often called God Ram, but he meant a God beyond all forms and names.

Many groups claim Kabir. Hindus sing his songs. Muslims honor him. His verses are in the Sikh Guru Granth Sahib. The Kabir Panth follows him as its founder. A story says Hindus and Muslims argued over his body, and found only flowers.

words.d: a 15th-century weaver poet of Varanasi, honored by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs

lessons.title: Tulsidas and Tukaram
lessons.mainIdea: Tulsidas in Hindi and Tukaram in Marathi carried bhakti to millions of homes.
reading: *Tulsidas* (c. 1532–1623) wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi. It retells the Ramayana as a song of devotion to Rama. The Hanuman Chalisa, forty verses to Hanuman that many Hindus recite daily, is traditionally credited to him.

*Tukaram* (17th century) was a grocer's son in Maharashtra. He sang abhangas, devotional songs, to Vithoba, a form of Krishna at Pandharpur. Every year, many pilgrims walk to Pandharpur singing the songs of Tukaram and other poet-saints.

Both poets wrote for ordinary people. Tulsidas said he wrote for his own heart's joy. Tukaram's songs were so loved that a story says his notebooks, thrown into a river, returned undamaged. Their songs remain part of daily Hindu life.

words.d: forty verses to Hanuman, traditionally credited to Tulsidas
